summary: For every fixed k >= 2 there are a constant c > 0 and a threshold R such that for all r >= R at least a proportion c of the partitions of {1, ..., r} into k nonempty classes have every class an MSTD set (more sums than differences). This proves the positive-proportion conjecture of Chu, Luntzlara, Miller and Shao; the case k = 2 is due to Asada, Manski, Miller and Suh. The new ingredient is a k-colouring of Z/2hZ, h odd, in which antipodal residues get different colours and every colour class has full modular sumset, laid periodically on both ends of the interval.
paste_summary: Proved. For every fixed k >= 2 there are c > 0 and R such that for all r >= R, at least a proportion c of the partitions of {1, ..., r} into k nonempty classes have every class an MSTD set (|A + A| > |A - A|). This settles the positive-proportion conjecture of Chu, Luntzlara, Miller and Shao for all k; the case k = 2 was known. The proof uses a periodic modular colouring of the two ends of the interval together with the fringe method.
caveat: Significance modest (review 0.35). Journal versions and the classical MSTD papers were not read in full; no proof for k >= 3 was found in a bounded search, and the ProbXiv record is open.
title: Positive proportion conjecture for partitions into MSTD subsets
source: Hung Viet Chu, Noah Luntzlara, Steven J. Miller and Lily Shao, “Infinite Families of Partitions into MSTD Subsets”, arXiv:1808.05460 (2019). (https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05460)
statement: A **$k$-decomposition into MSTD subsets** is a partition of $I_r=\{1,2,\ldots,r\}$ into $k$ subsets, each having more pairwise sums than pairwise differences. **Positive proportion conjecture.** For any finite $k\ge 2$, the proportion of $k$-decompositions of $I_r$ into MSTD subsets is bounded below by a positive constant. This would extend the known positive-constant lower bound for $k=2$ and give a uniform abundance result for decompositions into any fixed finite number of MSTD subsets; the source does not establish the conjecture for general $k$.
